facts.text: English needs only 26 letters, while Japanese students must learn about two thousand symbols to have the basic tools for reading and writing.
An alphabet uses symbols that show how words sound; Chinese characters show both the sound and the meaning of words.
Japanese uses two kana syllabaries, hiragana and katakana, each with 46 basic symbols; the kana were developed from Chinese characters.
Each kana symbol stands for one syllable; katakana is mainly used for words borrowed from other languages.
Japanese borrowed thousands of Chinese characters (kanji), each with its own meaning, and usually writes them mixed with hiragana.
Japan's official list of kanji for everyday use, issued in 2010, has 2,136 characters (up from 1,945; 196 added and 5 removed).
The Arabic alphabet has 28 letters: 25 consonants and 3 long vowels; it is read from right to left.
Arabic short vowels are shown by small marks above or below the letters, and these marks are rarely used in everyday writing.
Hindi is written in Devanagari, which is also used for Sanskrit and Marathi and is written from left to right.
In Devanagari every consonant letter includes a short 'a' sound, so the letter for k is read 'ka'; a vowel mark added to the consonant replaces that 'a'.
The University of Texas guide to the Hindi script lists 11 stand-alone vowels and 33 basic consonants, plus 7 dotted letters used mainly in borrowed words.
Derived: 11 vowels plus 33 consonants gives 44 basic Devanagari letters for Hindi.
King Sejong created the Korean alphabet, then called Hunminjeongeum, with 28 letters in 1443, tested it for three years and made it public in 1446.
Before Hangeul, writing Korean with Chinese characters was so hard that most Koreans could not read; Sejong made the alphabet so that ordinary people could easily learn to read and write.
Four of the original letters have dropped out of use, so modern Hangeul has 24 basic letters: 14 consonants and 10 vowels.
Hangeul letters are grouped into syllable blocks instead of being written in a single line as in European languages.
Since 1989 a literacy prize named after King Sejong has been awarded each year to people or groups that run successful literacy campaigns.
Taiwan's Ministry of Education lists 4,808 common characters (1982), 6,334 less common characters (1982) and 18,388 rare characters (1983).
Derived: Taiwan's three lists together hold 29,530 characters, and the rare list is almost four times as long as the common list.
Derived: Japanese hiragana has 46 basic symbols, 2 more than the 44 basic Devanagari letters and 20 more than the 26 letters of English.
The University of Texas guide says that, with a little effort, learners can get used to the new Devanagari letter shapes within a week or two.
A description of Hangeul quoted by the National Institute of Korean Language says a normal child can master it in about two weeks.
